newsitem.title: spain: Radical Basque leaders freed as ETA strikes again.
newsitem.headline: Radical Basque leaders freed as ETA strikes again.

text.p: Twenty-two leaders of the Basque separatist movement who were arrested two months ago during a wave of political violence, were freed on Wednesday after posting 29 million pesetas ($200,000) bail.
The release of the leaders of Herri Batasuna (HB), the political wing of Basque separatist group ETA, coincided with an attack on a prison worker by suspected rebel gunmen.
Juan Josee Baeza, 46, was shot and wounded outside his home in the Basque region minutes before the radicals left prison.
Government officials claimed victory after Herri Batasuna agreed to pay bail, reversing a policy of refusing to acknowledge the authority of Spanish state institutions.
But the Basque politicians, who were originally jailed for refusing to appear before the Supreme Court to answer charges of promoting violence, denied they had backed down.

"Although some want to say that it's a step backward for us, it's not. The Spanish judges are the ones who have taken a step backward," Herri Batasuna spokesman Floren Aoiz told Reuters just after leaving Madrid's Carabanchel prison.
"To pay the bail is to give a real slap in the face to the Spanish state."

Spanish Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja dismissed the claim as inflated and told a news conference that the separatist leaders had overestimated the size of the objection both in Spain and abroad to the court's decision to jail them.

"Whether or not there was some sort of political opportunity in the detention of the leadership HB, the final result is that Herri Batasuna had to obey the law, had to pay the bail, and had to introduce serious contradictions into its world," he said.
Four of the Herri Batasuna leaders had travelled to Belgium to avoid going to prison and to promote the idea that their colleagues were being jailed in an undemocratic state.
They returned last Friday and were arrested as they walked across the border with France in a dramatic bid for publicity.
On Monday, a Supreme Court judge reduced the bail on the 18 leaders orginally jailed and the party said it would now meet bail for the entire 22-member leadership.

The leaders of HB, which does not disavow violence as a means for achieving Basque independence, face trial in May for collaborating with an armed band, a charge that carries a prison penalty of six to 12 years.
The Supreme Court, which handles cases involving parliamentarians, began looking into Herri Batasuna's activities after it distributed a video promoting ETA during an election campaign last May.
The court decided that the video, along with published HB statements in defense of two assassinations that took place near the election, were grounds for filing charges.

At about the same time that the court began to take action against the separatist leaders, ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom), which has killed some 800 people since starting an independence drive in 1968, stepped up its violent activity.
ETA intensified deadly attacks, killing seven people in two months. A Herri Batasuna spokesman said the violence was partly a response to the jailing of the party's leadership.
Groups of youths supporting ETA started almost daily rampages through cities and towns in the northern region, throwing firebombs and smashing windows of state property.

The prison worker attacked on Wednesday escaped with his life, according to Basque police, only because he sensed he was about to be shot and turned his head. The bullet entered his neck at an angle that allowed him to flee.
